nodes.label: Skill: bootcamp-setup (tooling & MCP wiring, task 7.10)
nodes.rationale: Claude executes everything doable from the CLI; only identity-bound steps (accounts, key copying, browser OAuth) are left to the trainee.

nodes.label: Skill: defining-mvp (section 8, tasks 8.1-8.2)
nodes.rationale: First task of the bootcamp: the trainee's impression of the working method is formed here, so never ask him for formal wording.

nodes.label: Skill: defining-users (section 9, tasks 9.1-9.2)
nodes.rationale: Roles feed permission requirements and page restrictions; external services feed setup and the integration task.

nodes.label: Skill: writing-requirements (section 10, tasks 10.1-10.3)
nodes.rationale: Trainee supplies free-form notes; Claude formalises them to EARS/Gherkin standards and the trainee only reviews.

nodes.label: Skill: user-journey (section 11, tasks 11.1-11.2)
nodes.rationale: A canonical text structure is required so the text-to-activity-diagram conversion comes out clean.

nodes.label: Skill: designing-screens (section 12, tasks 12.1-12.4)
nodes.rationale: Only design-system components cross into the project; generated screens stay visual references, so the skill pushes for a rich design system.

nodes.label: Skill: drawio (native .drawio diagram generation & export)
nodes.rationale: Generic diagram engine invoked by other skills; XML is generated directly because Mermaid/CSV need server-side conversion.

nodes.label: Skill: building-features (section 14 seven tasks + section 13 modelling)
nodes.rationale: Claude builds and tests; the trainee steers, approves and tries the UI. Plan mode plus a jargon-free summary precede every task.

nodes.label: Skill: testing-and-security (section 15, tasks 15.1-15.3)
nodes.rationale: Per-feature testing belongs to building-features; this round asks a different question - do the features work together, and is the unauthorised actor actually blocked.

nodes.label: Skill: deploying (section 16, tasks 16.1-16.3, Vercel)
nodes.rationale: Deploy the pipeline before the product: in the reference project deployment came last, the session ran out and the trainer finished it himself.

Tool: context7 MCP (user scope, ctx7sk- key, connected before any coding)
nodes.rationale: Fetches up-to-date library/framework docs so generated code matches current versions; user scope because it helps all the trainee's projects, and a key avoids the anonymous rate limit.

nodes.label: Tool: Supabase project (Postgres + built-in auth, Free plan)
nodes.rationale: Gives a database and a ready-made login system together, with no Docker and no local install, and behaves identically in dev and after deployment. The DB password is shown once only - copy and store it now.

nodes.label: Tool: Supabase MCP (project scope, OAuth, read-only off, Storage off)
nodes.rationale: Lets Claude create tables and read DB logs directly so the trainee never opens the Supabase console to write SQL; project scope (or project_ref) keeps his other projects out of reach and no personal access token is needed.

nodes.label: Tool: chrome-devtools MCP (connected at task 14.2, browser testing)
nodes.rationale: Deferred out of day 1 to spread setup effort; every connected integration inflates every message and burns the trainee's credit.

nodes.label: Tool: Vercel MCP (https://mcp.vercel.com - project mgmt, deploy logs)
nodes.rationale: Reads deployment logs so failures are diagnosed instead of guessed; Claude Code is an officially supported client.

nodes.label: Tool: Vercel CLI (login, link, env add, --prod)
nodes.rationale: Does the actual deploy and sets env vars, because the MCP has no environment-variable tools yet.

nodes.label: Tool: GitHub repository (created at task 14.1)
Tool: Claude Design (design system + screen generation)
Tool: DesignSync (/design-sync - pulls one component at a time)
Tool: draw.io (activity diagram; added to the tools table at section 11)
Governing principle: the trainee gives raw input, Claude does the formal wording
nodes.rationale: Asking a beginner for formal phrasing fails to teach the method; he describes in his own words and then reviews Claude's structured output.

nodes.label: Rule: never ask the trainee to read code, open a file, or run a test
nodes.rationale: He verifies through the UI and through Claude's plain-language report only.

nodes.label: Rule: testing is Claude's job after every feature
Rule: plan mode plus a jargon-free 'what we build now' summary before every task
Rule: a pasted key goes into the command or .env only, never echoed, .env in .gitignore
nodes.rationale: Write 'key received' in the history instead of the value; the document-everything rule does not cover secrets.

nodes.label: Rule: add each newly used tool to PRODUCT.md section 10 immediately, not at the end
Rule: rewrite the PRODUCT.md section in place and update the CLAUDE.md progress ledger
nodes.rationale: Also remind the trainee to commit and push - documents are saved like code is.

nodes.label: Rule: report in non-technical language, no function names or status codes
Boundary table: Claude runs the CLI, the trainee does identity-bound steps (/mcp Authenticate)
nodes.rationale: The interactive browser OAuth flow needs the trainee's own identity and cannot be executed by Claude; detect the OS before issuing any command instead of assuming Windows or macOS.

nodes.label: Warning: a newly added MCP server does not work in the current session - restart Claude Code
nodes.rationale: If you do not say this, the trainee will read the normal state as a failed connection.

nodes.label: Ordering rule: create the Supabase project before wiring the Supabase MCP
nodes.rationale: The MCP needs an existing project to point at; verify the link afterwards by actually querying his tables.

nodes.label: Rule: defer chrome-devtools (14.2) and Vercel MCP (16.2) - each connection inflates every message
Artifact: problem + goal + 3-5 objectives extracted from free-form speech
Artifact: three scope lists - in scope, out of scope, future development plan
Rule: derive in-scope items from the 8.1 description, do not re-collect them
nodes.rationale: The trainee's own description of his product's pages already is the scope list before it is formalised - which is why 8.2 depends on 8.1.

nodes.label: Quality check: the problem must be a problem, not a solution
nodes.rationale: 'I want a booking app' describes a solution - step back and ask what goes wrong today without it.

nodes.label: Quality check: objectives must be concrete - reject easy/fast/better without a metric
nodes.rationale: Never wave weak wording through out of politeness - naming an unmeasurable objective is a service to the trainee.

nodes.label: Warning: an empty out-of-scope list is the single most common mistake
nodes.rationale: Anything not explicitly ruled out comes back later as somebody's demand.

nodes.label: Rule: keep 3-5 core areas; move the overflow to the future plan, not the bin
nodes.rationale: Do not refuse or delete unilaterally - order the list by closeness to the core journey and ask which one, if absent, makes the product meaningless. The real reason is finishing inside bootcamp time; say it plainly.

nodes.label: Mistake: confusing an objective (measured by impact) with a scope item (measured by being built); scope must not describe technologies
nodes.rationale: 'A database' is not a scope item - scope describes what the user does.

nodes.label: Default technical decision: one User entity + a role field
nodes.rationale: Simplest for bootcamp products and lets one person hold more than one role; separate entities only when the stored data differs fundamentally, and then say why. Never discuss tables or keys with the trainee - defer to section 13.

nodes.label: Mandatory question: can one person hold two roles, and what must he never do to himself
nodes.rationale: In the real build this was never asked, so a service provider could book his own appointments; it surfaced only during building and then needed blocking in both the UI and the server. The answer becomes a permission rule at task 14.3.

nodes.label: Rule: rewrite a need stated as a feature back into a need
nodes.rationale: A need survives a design change; a feature does not.

nodes.label: Rule: for every external service ask how it will actually work, not just its name
nodes.rationale: In the real build one question about the meeting mechanism (must the host admit every joiner manually?) changed the product structure: each provider now connects his own account and hosts his own meetings. Ask who owns the account, what the user actually sees, and whether the connection is per-user or one for the whole product; record what each service does, who connects it and what it needs.

nodes.label: Concept: the system itself is an actor when things happen with nobody pressing a button
nodes.rationale: Needed later as a lane in the user-journey diagram (section 11); forgetting it is a listed common mistake.

nodes.label: Standard: EARS patterns (ubiquitous / event-driven / state-driven / unwanted behaviour)
nodes.rationale: Requirements are never written in plain prose; shall = mandatory, should = desirable, will = a statement of fact and not a requirement.

nodes.label: Rule: flat numeric IDs FR-1 / NFR-1, never nested ones like HOME-NAV-001
Format: Gherkin acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then) on every requirement
nodes.rationale: Each requirement is written complete in one place (EARS + user story + acceptance criteria + priority); tables are only an index of id and title.

nodes.label: Quality gate: necessary, atomic, verifiable, clear
Warning: check a self-proposed rule against earlier decisions before showing it
nodes.rationale: It really happened: an automatic skip-the-weekend rule was proposed although an earlier requirement let the provider choose his own working days; it was caught only because the trainer read the suggestion against what had been agreed. Always state where a proposed requirement was derived from, and name the conflict instead of stepping over it silently.

nodes.label: Rule: propose NFRs without being asked - the trainee never will
nodes.rationale: Even the trainer, a software engineer, did not notice they were missing; they were written because the standard demands them. Every NFR needs a metric - 'fast' is a wish, 'within two seconds' is a requirement.

nodes.label: Non-negotiable baseline: hashed passwords, secrets in env vars not in the repo
IA rule: the summary location holds a preview, the dedicated section holds the full data
Mistake list: requirement restates a scope item, untestable criteria, every priority 10/10, two behaviours in one requirement, NFR with no number
nodes.rationale: Scope says what we build, a requirement says how the system behaves.

nodes.label: Canonical journey block: Journey / Actor / Start / numbered steps / Decision / End
nodes.rationale: One numbered step = one action or one decision; every branch needs a go-to target; one actor per journey block; never drop a step the trainee mentioned, and suggest a missing one rather than adding it silently.

nodes.label: Warning: the trainee always describes the happy path - ask for the four branch cases
nodes.rationale: Not signed in, item not found or unavailable, wrong input, went back or abandoned midway. A journey of eight steps with zero decisions is probably incomplete.

nodes.label: Warning: after an interruption (login, payment, permission) ask where the user returns
nodes.rationale: In the real build 'then back to the chosen service' became an explicit journey point because the trainer insisted; without it the user would be lost after signing in.

nodes.label: Rule: a lane per party including the system, but swap lanes for colours if it gets crowded
nodes.rationale: Readability beats completeness, and the trainer literally asked for it that way - preferred shape plus a fallback. Present the diagram as an image so the trainee never opens a file.

nodes.label: Limit: the diagram proves the steps are correct, not that they feel comfortable
nodes.rationale: A step can be perfectly right and still look broken - booking took a noticeable time before the success message, so a waiting layer was added. Watch for any step that waits on an external service and offer a loading indicator yourself.

nodes.label: Hard limit: DesignSync moves components, generated screens never transfer
nodes.rationale: Technical and not negotiable - so push for a rich design system, since components are the only thing that crosses into the project. Never promise the screens will be imported.

nodes.label: Rule: the Claude Design project must be of type Design System - the type is fixed at creation
nodes.rationale: A normal project can never become a design system; catch it now, not a week later - it is a late-discovered mistake that costs a rebuild.

nodes.label: Rule: Claude writes the design prompts (system prompt + one per screen, identical token values)
nodes.rationale: Screens generated with different values come out inconsistent; list the components explicitly instead of saying 'ready-made components'.

nodes.label: Rule: research established conventions before prompting (landing, dashboard, pricing)
nodes.rationale: A minute of research beats three correction rounds; in the real build research changed the landing-page section list and dropped the testimonials section because an MVP has no customers yet.

nodes.label: Mandatory: ask the trainee to copy his answers to Claude Design's questions
nodes.rationale: You only know what you prompted; details the trainee added in the form look like noise at build time and get discarded - exactly the decisions he took deliberately get lost. Ask before generation and again after each screen.

nodes.label: Delivery: share link by default, download screen files when one of three conditions hits
nodes.rationale: Ask for the download yourself when your result does not match his description, when the screen has many states (a calendar), or when it is crowded - do not wait for him to diagnose it. Clean up design-temp/ after building.

nodes.label: Split: Claude Design draws visual states, behaviour and logic are built in code
nodes.rationale: The real calendar was designed with its visual states (year/month pick, disabled cells, pressure colouring) while navigation logic and the booking horizon were implemented later in code - do not stuff behaviour into a design prompt.

nodes.label: Rule: every screen must trace back to a journey step or a requirement
nodes.rationale: Record name, path and who reaches it - the last one becomes a permission constraint at task 14.3, so never leave it blank.

nodes.label: draw.io: native mxGraphModel XML with root cells id=0 and id=1
nodes.rationale: Always generate XML directly - Mermaid and CSV need server-side conversion and cannot be saved as native files. Missing root cells render a blank diagram; a self-closing edge cell renders no edge.

nodes.label: Critical: never emit XML comments; escape special chars; unique cell ids
nodes.rationale: Comments waste tokens and can cause parse errors that produce an empty or corrupt export.

nodes.label: draw.io: export png/svg/pdf with --embed-diagram, then delete the .drawio source
nodes.rationale: The exported file carries the full diagram XML so it stays editable in draw.io; if the CLI is missing, keep the .drawio file and point at app.diagrams.net.

nodes.label: Cycle: design-sync a piece, build UI+server wired to the DB, test, trainee tries, commit
nodes.rationale: Never build a whole task in one go - feature by feature, committing after each one and not only at day end.

nodes.label: Three test layers after every feature: repeatable automated cases, CLI checks, chrome-devtools browser walk
nodes.rationale: Then report non-technically; stop any test server explicitly so the trainee does not hit a port-occupied error when he runs the app himself.

nodes.label: Repo creation: leave README / .gitignore / license unchecked (merge-conflict warning)
nodes.rationale: GitHub's own docs warn that selecting them when pushing an existing project creates a merge conflict; Claude creates those files locally instead. Private is enough, and the repo URL goes into CLAUDE.md.

nodes.label: Modelling: extract entities from requirements and roles - ask what the system must remember
nodes.rationale: Keys and join tables are Claude's job, not the trainee's - create the join table and explain it in one sentence rather than passing it silently. Explain every entity in a sentence so he knows what he is approving. Common modelling errors: an entity that stores nothing meaningful, a relation with no defined type, a table created for a single value that settings could hold.

nodes.label: Warning: open every ERD box and confirm its fields are written inside before showing it
nodes.rationale: In the real build some boxes came out empty while the diagram looked fine from a distance - correct structure, missing content.

nodes.label: Rule: after creating the tables, redraw the ERD from the real tables, not from the written model
nodes.rationale: A diagram that does not match reality is worse than none, because the trainee will trust it while it is wrong.

nodes.label: Warning: no error message does not mean it worked - verify the output itself
nodes.rationale: In a real build the table-provisioning tool never ran at all and emitted no error, so the database stayed empty and it was found only by looking inside it.

nodes.label: Rule: enforce restrictions on the server, not by hiding UI elements
nodes.rationale: Hiding a button does not stop the function being called directly; test with every role and try a forbidden page as each of them. Ask explicitly for every logical rule: can role X do something it makes no sense for it to do?

nodes.label: Warning: a permission denial must return the right forbidden code, not a generic 500
nodes.rationale: In the real build the block worked but reported the wrong thing - the denial surfaced as a server error.

nodes.label: Warning: native date/time/number inputs render in the OS language - use text fields with a fixed pattern
nodes.rationale: Arabic digits and month names appeared on an Arabic machine; use YYYY-MM-DD text inputs with simple validation. Restated in testing-and-security 2.3 as something only a browser test reveals.

nodes.label: Rule: if login is demanded mid-flow, return the user to where he was
nodes.rationale: Also decide explicitly what a signed-out visitor sees, and test in a signed-out session rather than your own signed-in one.

nodes.label: Rule: external-service console steps get numbered clicks and every term explained; on confusion split further
nodes.rationale: The trainer literally said 'I did not understand you at all' twice in a row at this stage - never assume he knows what an OAuth client, a scope or a redirect URI is, and never just re-word the same explanation.

nodes.label: Rule: after the first successful integration expect gaps - walk the whole journey, not just the connection
nodes.rationale: Typical misses: a notification to the second party, a redirect after completion, a missing field in a message. If the product needs no external service, say so explicitly and spend the time on remaining scope instead of inventing an integration.

nodes.label: Rule: expect corrections once the dashboard is seen - treat them as part of building
nodes.rationale: In the real build the trainer asked to hide a whole page from two roles after seeing it; seeing the dashboard reveals what discussion does not.

nodes.label: Value of section 15: test chains, not single functions (create-edit-cancel, contention, dependency)
nodes.rationale: Real example: booking the same slot twice was rejected even under a different service of the same provider - invisible to a single-feature test, found only by a scenario crossing two services of one person. After a cancel, verify the state really returned (is the resource available again?).

nodes.label: Mandatory error cases: no login, bad input, missing resource, missing permission, repeated operation
nodes.rationale: A product that works when everything goes right has not been tested yet.

nodes.label: Rule: walk the journey in the browser via chrome-devtools, not from the CLI alone
nodes.rationale: Some defects exist only in what the user sees - the OS-language digits and month names showed up in no server-side check.

nodes.label: Rule: after each fix rerun the scenario and say so in the report
nodes.rationale: You do not know you fixed it until the scenario passes.

nodes.label: Warning: 'permissions are applied' is a claim, not a test result - attempt and report the outcome
nodes.rationale: Sign in as every role, actually try what must be blocked (including seeing another user's data within the same role) and write what happened: 'I signed in as a consumer and tried to open the admin page - I was blocked.'

nodes.label: Rule: verify the basics - hashed passwords, keys in .env, .env gitignored, business rules server-side
nodes.rationale: Check them for real and state the result, because the trainee will not open a file to confirm.

nodes.label: Honesty rule: admit the reference project never completed repeatable automated tests
nodes.rationale: It relied on the CLI and the browser, which cost manual retesting after every change and left no guard against a fixed defect returning - that felt absence is exactly why writing them after each feature became the rule. Do not pretend otherwise if the trainee asks.

nodes.label: Gate: do not move to deployment while any scenario still fails - say so explicitly
Two separate deployment moments: day 3 (16.1+16.2) and day 10 (16.3)
nodes.rationale: We deploy the pipeline before the product: in the reference project deployment came last, the session did not finish and the trainer completed it himself, so any breakage on the way would have surfaced at the worst possible time. Never repeat 16.1 on day 10 - it confuses the trainee into thinking something broke.

nodes.label: Tool split: Vercel MCP manages and diagnoses, the CLI deploys and sets env vars
nodes.rationale: The MCP has no environment-variable tools yet, so the two are used together and neither replaces the other.

nodes.label: Rule: set the root directory and add production env vars before deploying, not after
nodes.rationale: Otherwise the deploy succeeds and the product breaks at runtime. Also confirm .vercel is in .gitignore before any push, and verify the auth check actually passes rather than assuming it.

nodes.label: Warning: tell the trainee in advance the first URL will look empty - the outcome is that it opened
nodes.rationale: On day 3 there is a skeleton, not a product, and he does not know that - he may read the near-empty page as a failed deploy.

nodes.label: Rule: when a deploy fails, read the log via Vercel MCP and summarise - never guess, never hand over the raw log
nodes.rationale: He reads neither code nor logs - you read, he reads your summary of what failed, why, and what you will do.

nodes.label: Warning: after deploy, update external-service redirect/callback and CORS URLs to production
nodes.rationale: The single most common post-deploy breakage - the service works locally and fails on the live link. Better still, register both the local and the production callback back at task 14.7, since the production URL is known from day 3 and most providers accept several.

nodes.label: Rule: verify on the production URL itself - 'works on my machine' is not evidence
nodes.rationale: Walk a full journey on the live link including login and any external service, then report the result.

nodes.label: Rule: after the first success every redeploy is just vercel --prod - do not wait for day 10
nodes.rationale: Task 16.3 is the final redeploy, not the only one.

nodes.label: Final audit: deployment adds the last tool, so review the whole tools table before the review section
nodes.rationale: Compare the table against what was actually used, ask the trainee explicitly about his product's own external services (payment, maps, mail, messaging) since only he knows their purpose in his words, and make sure purposes are written in his language because he presents every line.

nodes.label: Five real deployment obstacles to pre-empt (stalling in the dashboard, auth check failure, missing root dir or keys, stale callback URLs, committed .vercel)
nodes.rationale: All five actually happened in a real run; lead the steps yourself instead of letting the trainee search the Vercel dashboard.
